title: 1 Chronicles 23:7–23
context: This section lists the Levite family heads under the three sons of Levi, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari (compare Numbers 3:17). Within the Kohathites, Aaron and his sons are set apart to sanctify the most holy things, burn incense, minister, and bless in the LORD’s name, while the sons of Moses are counted among the tribe of Levi rather than the priesthood. Some names and relationships are hard to trace: two lists of the sons of Shimei appear in verses 9 and 10, and the second son of Shimei is Zina in verse 10 and Zizah in verse 11. Some names also appear in slightly different forms in the parallel list of 24:20–31. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the list as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to families across generations and the distinct callings he gives within one people.

verses.text: Of the Gershonites: Ladan and Shimei.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Gershonites listed through Ladan and Shimei. Each family has a recognized place in the service of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the genealogy as preserving the identity of those called to serve. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the beginning of a careful record.

verses.text: The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the chief, Zetham, and Joel, three.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the sons of Ladan, with Jehiel as chief. Leadership within families helps order the work of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the naming of a chief as part of God’s provision for orderly service. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that structure serves worship.

verses.text: The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the heads of the fathers’ households of Ladan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see three sons of Shimei named as heads of the households of Ladan. The relationships in the list are not always easy to trace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as preserving names that mattered for service, even when details are hard to follow. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact family connections with caution.

verses.text: The sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see four sons of Shimei listed: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. Each name represents a family called to serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated attention to names as reflecting God’s care for individuals within his people. Both traditions commonly note that Zina appears as Zizah in the next verse.

verses.text: Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second; but Jeush and Beriah didn’t have many sons; therefore they became a fathers’ house in one reckoning.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Jeush and Beriah had few sons, so they were counted as one household. Practical adjustments serve the work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the arrangement as wise flexibility within God’s order. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that smaller families still had a place in service.

verses.text: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Kohath listed: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. This branch includes the priestly line.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Kohathites as specially significant because Aaron and Moses come from them. Both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a central family.

verses.text: The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses; and Aaron was separated that he should sanctify the most holy things, he and his sons forever, to burn incense before the LORD, to minister to him, and to bless in his name forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Aaron and his sons set apart to sanctify the most holy things, burn incense, minister, and bless in the LORD’s name. Their calling is a gift and a responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign appointment of the priestly line (compare Exodus 28:1; Numbers 6:23). Readers in both traditions commonly see the priesthood as pointing forward to Christ and to the calling of God’s people (compare 1 Peter 2:5).

verses.text: But as for Moses the man of God, his sons were named among the tribe of Levi.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sons of Moses were counted among the tribe of Levi, not the priesthood. Even the great leader’s family serves without special status.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the distinction as showing that God’s appointment, not family prominence, determines priestly office. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a lesson in humility.

verses.text: The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Moses named as Gershom and Eliezer. Their names recall God’s help in Moses’ life (compare Exodus 2:22; 18:4).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the names as memorials of God’s faithfulness in the past. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as connecting later Levites with earlier history.

verses.text: The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Shebuel named as chief of the sons of Gershom. Leadership continues quietly in the family line of Moses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continuation of Moses’ family in service as a quiet sign of God’s faithfulness. Both traditions commonly note that the name appears in a slightly different form, Shubael, in 24:20.

verses.text: The son of Eliezer was Rehabiah the chief; and Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Eliezer had only one son, Rehabiah, yet Rehabiah’s descendants were very many. Small beginnings can lead to great growth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God multiplying a family as an expression of his blessing. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as encouragement that God can bring much from little.

verses.text: The son of Izhar: Shelomith the chief.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Shelomith named as chief of the sons of Izhar. Each family branch has recognized leadership for its work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the naming of chiefs as part of an ordered community. Both traditions commonly note that the name appears as Shelomoth in 24:22.

verses.text: The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Hebron ranked first through fourth. The ordering helps assign responsibilities fairly and clearly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see careful ranking as part of the orderliness of worship. Readers in both traditions commonly note that the same names appear in 24:23.

verses.text: The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief, and Isshiah the second.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Uzziel listed, with Micah as chief and Isshiah second. Each family has a defined role in service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as preserving God’s ordering of his servants. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a coherent record of service.

verses.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Merari listed, Mahli and Mushi, with Mahli’s sons Eleazar and Kish. The third branch of Levi is now in view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Merarites as completing the picture of Levi’s families. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the structured genealogy.

verses.text: Eleazar died, and had no sons, but daughters only; and their relatives, the sons of Kish, took them as wives.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Eleazar died with daughters only, who married their relatives, the sons of Kish. Family lines are preserved through such marriages.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the arrangement as consistent with the law on daughters’ inheritance (compare Numbers 27:8; 36:8). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a practical provision for continuity.

verses.text: The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Mushi listed as Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth. Even the smallest branches of the family are recorded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completeness of the list as reflecting God’s care for all his servants. Readers in both traditions commonly note that Jeremoth appears as Jerimoth in 24:30.
